pos: v.t. (to clear from a charge, to declare not guilty; used in Scripture chiefly in the negative, of what God will not do with the wicked)
etymology: Old French aquiter, to settle a claim, from Latin ad and quietare, to quiet. To acquit is to declare a charge settled — which is why the doctrine of justification turns on the word.
biblical_def: Both occurrences are negative, and both are theological. Job says of himself: “If I sin, then thou markest me, and thou wilt not acquit me from mine iniquity” (Job 10:14). Nahum says it of God's dealing with the world: “The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet” (Nahum 1:3). The same clause stands in the great self-revelation at Sinai, where mercy and justice are declared in a single breath: God is “forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty” (Exodus 34:7). Two things are asserted together that human courts cannot hold together, and the whole difficulty of the gospel lies here. God forgives, and God does not acquit the guilty. Paul's answer to how both can be true is the centre of Romans: the cross was set forth “that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). Not an acquittal of the guilty as though they were innocent, but a righteous justification purchased at a price.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines acquit as to set free or judicially to clear from an accusation, and notes it is followed by of before the crime.
webster_full: ACQUIT, v.t. To set free; to release or discharge from an obligation, accusation, guilt, censure, suspicion, or whatever lies upon a person as a charge or duty.
2. To clear; to release; to absolve; with of before the crime.
ACQUITTAL, n. A judicial setting free, or deliverance from the charge of an offense.
JUSTIFY, v.t. In theology, to pardon and clear from guilt; to absolve or acquit from guilt and merited punishment.
GUILTY, a. Justly chargeable with a crime; criminal; not innocent.
scriptures: Nahum 1:3
The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
Exodus 34:7

Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation.
If I sin, then thou markest me, and thou wilt not acquit me from mine iniquity.
Romans 3:26
To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.
corruption_summary: Forgiveness is imagined as God overlooking sin, which Exodus 34:7 expressly denies in the same sentence where He proclaims His mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular account of divine forgiveness is that God, being loving, does not hold sin against people — that He simply declines to press the charge. Exodus 34:7 makes that impossible. In the very sentence where God proclaims Himself as forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, He adds and that will by no means clear the guilty. Both halves are His self-description. A God who acquitted the wicked would be an unjust judge, and Proverbs says that he that justifieth the wicked is an abomination to the LORD. This is precisely why the atonement is not an optional theory: sin is not waived, it is paid, and the doctrine that Christ bore the penalty in the place of His people is the only account that lets Exodus 34:7 stand whole.

The opposite error hears will not at all acquit the wicked and concludes that no assurance is possible. Nahum 1:3 begins with the LORD is slow to anger, and the preceding verse says He reserveth wrath for His enemies — a distinction is being drawn, not a universal sentence pronounced. The believer is not acquitted in the sense of being called innocent; he is justified, declared righteous on the ground of a righteousness not his own, with the penalty already borne. That is a stronger footing than acquittal, because an acquittal can be reopened by new evidence and a satisfied debt cannot.
roots_summary: Hebrew naqah, to be clean or free from punishment — Nahum 1:3, Exodus 34:7, Job 10:14; Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify or declare righteous — Romans 3:26.
roots_lines: Hebrew naqah — to be clean, to be held innocent, to go unpunished; rendered acquit and clear in Nahum 1:3 and Exodus 34:7.
Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous; Romans 3:24, 3:26, and throughout the argument of Romans and Galatians.
Greek hilasterion (G2435) — propitiation, mercy seat; Romans 3:25, the ground on which God can be just and justifier.
Hebrew chanun and rachum — gracious and merciful; the opening terms of Exodus 34:6-7, which end with the guilty uncleared.
Proverbs 17:15 states the principle a judge is bound by: he that justifieth the wicked… even they both are abomination to the LORD.
usage: “Will not at all acquit the wicked” — and the same verse begins slow to anger.
“Forgiving iniquity… and that will by no means clear the guilty” — both in one sentence.
“Just, and the justifier” — the gospel's answer to how both can stand.

pos: v.t. and n. (to deliver by force from danger or captivity; used of David recovering the captives, of a people saving Jonathan, and of God whom none can resist)
etymology: Old French rescourre, from Latin re and excutere, to shake out. Rescue implies force: it is not persuasion or ransom but taking back by strength what an enemy holds.
biblical_def: David at Ziklag is the pattern: “And David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away: and David rescued his two wives” (1 Samuel 30:18). The whole company was taken and the whole company was brought back. The word also describes a congregation overruling its king: when Saul had sworn Jonathan must die for tasting honey, “the people said unto Saul, Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid… So the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not” (1 Samuel 14:45). David prays for it in a psalm: “Lord, how long wilt thou look on? rescue my soul from their destructions, my darling from the lions” (Psalm 35:17). And the most sobering use inverts it — when God is the one taking away, no rescue exists: “I will be unto Ephraim as a lion… I will take away, and none shall rescue him” (Hosea 5:14). The covenant curse of Deuteronomy says the same of a people under judgment: “thy sheep shall be given unto thine enemies, and thou shalt have none to rescue them” (Deuteronomy 28:31). Rescue is always by a stronger hand, and against the strongest there is none.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rescue as to free or deliver from confinement, violence, danger or evil, and notes it implies force or open violence.
webster_full: RESCUE, v.t. To free or deliver from confinement, violence, danger or evil.
2. To retake; to take from an enemy by force.
RESCUE, n. The act of rescuing; deliverance from restraint, violence or danger; liberation from actual force.
RECOVER, v.t. To regain; to get or obtain that which was lost.
DELIVER, v.t. To free; to release, as from restraint; to set at liberty.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 30:18
And David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away: and David rescued his two wives.
Psalm 35:17
Lord, how long wilt thou look on? rescue my soul from their destructions, my darling from the lions.
1 Samuel 14:45

And the people said unto Saul, Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid: as the LORD liveth, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he hath wrought with God this day. So the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not.
Hosea 5:14
For I will be unto Ephraim as a lion, and as a young lion to the house of Judah: I, even I, will tear and go away; I will take away, and none shall rescue him.
corruption_summary: Salvation is described as an offer of assistance to people in difficulty, and the biblical word means taking captives back by force.
corruption_paragraphs: Rescue implies three things the modern gospel presentation often omits: a real captor, real captives who cannot free themselves, and a rescuer strong enough to take them back. David did not negotiate with the Amalekites; he pursued and recovered. Where salvation is preached as an offer of help to people who are merely struggling, the doctrine of total depravity has gone quietly missing, and with it the necessity of a monergistic deliverance. Scripture's picture is of men taken captive by the devil at his will, delivered from the power of darkness and translated into the kingdom of God's dear Son. That is a rescue, and the rescued contribute nothing to it but their captivity.

Hosea 5:14 supplies the warning that the word cuts both ways. When God Himself is the lion, none shall rescue. There is no higher court, no stronger arm, no appeal. The comfort of Romans 8 — who shall separate us from the love of Christ — rests on the same fact from the other side: the hand that holds the believer is the hand nothing can pry open. The doctrine of God's omnipotence is a terror to His enemies and the only real security His people have, and both follow from the same sentence.
roots_summary: Hebrew natsal, to snatch away, deliver — Psalm 35:17, Hosea 5:14, Deuteronomy 28:31; padah, to ransom — 1 Samuel 14:45; Greek exaireo (G1807), to take out — Acts 23:27, Galatians 1:4.
roots_lines: Hebrew natsal — to strip, snatch away, deliver; the common word behind rescue and deliver.
Hebrew padah — to ransom, to redeem by payment; 1 Samuel 14:45, of the people redeeming Jonathan.
Greek exaireo (G1807) — to take out, to rescue; Acts 23:27 of Paul taken from the mob, Galatians 1:4 of deliverance from this present evil world.
Greek ruomai (G4506) — to draw to oneself, to rescue; Colossians 1:13, delivered us from the power of darkness.
Colossians 1:13 gives the gospel in the vocabulary of rescue: delivered us from the power of darkness, and translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son.
usage: “David recovered all… and David rescued his two wives” — pursuit, not negotiation.
“Rescue my soul from their destructions” — the prayer of a man who cannot free himself.
“I will take away, and none shall rescue him” — against that hand there is no rescue.

pos: n. (a temporary intermission or delay; the pause Pharaoh used to harden himself, and the seven days Jabesh asked for)
etymology: Old French respit, from Latin respectus, a looking back or regard — hence a delay granted. A respite is not a reprieve: the thing is postponed, not cancelled.
biblical_def: After the plague of frogs Moses prayed, and the frogs died, and the land stank. “But when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart, and hearkened not unto them; as the LORD had said” (Exodus 8:15). The sequence is exact and it recurs through the plague narrative: pressure, promise, relief, hardening. The mercy that removes an affliction is the very thing Pharaoh uses to return to his sin, and the closing clause — as the LORD had said — notes that God had announced this in advance. The other use is a request made in desperation: Nahash the Ammonite had offered Jabesh-gilead terms involving the loss of every right eye, and “the elders of Jabesh said unto him, Give us seven days' respite, that we may send messengers unto all the coasts of Israel: and then, if there be no man to save us, we will come out to thee” (1 Samuel 11:3). The seven days were granted, Saul heard, and the city was delivered. One respite was used to look for a saviour; the other was used to harden a heart. The pause itself decided nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines respite as a temporary intermission of labor or of any process, an interval of rest, and in law a temporary suspension of the execution of a sentence.
webster_full: RESPITE, n. Pause; temporary intermission of labor, or of any process or operation; interval of rest.
2. In law, a temporary suspension of the execution of a capital sentence.
3. Delay; forbearance; prolongation of time for the payment of a debt.
REPRIEVE, n. The suspension of the execution of a sentence for a time.
FORBEARANCE, n. The exercise of patience; long suffering; indulgence toward those who injure us.
scriptures: Exodus 8:15
But when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart, and hearkened not unto them; as the LORD had said.
1 Samuel 11:3
And the elders of Jabesh said unto him, Give us seven days' respite, that we may send messengers unto all the coasts of Israel: and then, if there be no man to save us, we will come out to thee.
Nahum 1:3
The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
Romans 3:26
To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.
corruption_summary: Delay in judgment is read as evidence that judgment is not coming, and Exodus shows a man drawing exactly that inference and destroying himself with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Pharaoh's reasoning in Exodus 8:15 is the reasoning of every age. The frogs are gone; therefore the crisis is over; therefore nothing needs to change. Peter answers the same inference in his own day: scoffers say all things continue as they were from the beginning, and he replies that the Lord is not slack concerning His promise but is longsuffering, not willing that any should perish. The delay is mercy, and it is mercy with a purpose — space to repent. Treating the space as proof that there is nothing to repent of turns the kindest thing God does into the instrument of a man's hardening. Romans 2:4 states it exactly: the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance, and the man who despises it treasures up wrath.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what Jabesh-gilead did with its seven days. They did not use the respite to negotiate better terms or to persuade themselves the Ammonite was bluffing; they spent it sending messengers to look for a saviour, having already agreed that if none came they would submit. That is the right use of a delay, and it is a fair picture of the interval every hearer of the gospel is living in. The pause is real, it is limited, and its whole value lies in whom one spends it looking for.
roots_summary: Hebrew revachah, respite or relief — Exodus 8:15, Lamentations 3:56; raphah in the sense of slackening — 1 Samuel 11:3.
roots_lines: Hebrew revachah — a breathing space, relief; Exodus 8:15, and Lamentations 3:56 of a cry for relief.
Hebrew ravach — to be wide, to have room, hence to have relief; the root of the noun.
Hebrew Nahash — the Ammonite king whose terms occasioned the request at Jabesh.
Hebrew Jabesh-gilead — the city Saul delivered, and which later buried his bones with honour.
Romans 2:4 names the danger in the delay: despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering?
usage: “When Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart” — mercy turned into an occasion.
“Give us seven days' respite, that we may send messengers” — a pause spent looking for a saviour.
A respite postpones; it does not cancel.

pos: n. (a grave offence; in Job an act for the judges, in Ezekiel the bloodshed that fills a land, and in Acts the charge a Roman must face)
etymology: Latin crimen, an accusation or charge, later the offence charged. The Authorized Version uses it sparingly and always for offences of the gravest kind — never for a mere fault.
biblical_def: Job, defending his integrity, names adultery as an offence belonging to the civil magistrate as well as to God: “For this is an heinous crime; yea, it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges” (Job 31:11). Ezekiel describes a whole society: “Make a chain: for the land is full of bloody crimes, and the city is full of violence” (Ezekiel 7:23), with the sentence following — “I will bring the worst of the heathen, and they shall possess their houses” (Ezekiel 7:24). The chain is for captivity. The New Testament uses are procedural and both come from Festus. Explaining Roman practice to Agrippa: “It is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die, before that he which is accused have the accusers face to face, and have licence to answer for himself concerning the crime laid against him” (Acts 25:16). And, unable to state a charge: “For it seemeth to me unreasonable to send a prisoner, and not withal to signify the crimes laid against him” (Acts 25:27). A pagan governor articulates the rule of law — face your accusers, know the charge, answer for yourself — and Luke records it without irony.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines crime as an act which violates a law, divine or human, and notes that crime and vice differ, the former being a violation of law.
webster_full: CRIME, n. An act which violates a law, divine or human; an act which violates a rule of moral duty; an offense against the laws of right.
2. Any great wickedness; iniquity; wrong.
HEINOUS, a. Hateful; odious; hence, great, enormous; atrocious; as a heinous crime.
MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government of some branch of it.
ACCUSER, n. One who accuses or blames; an officer who prefers an accusation against another.
scriptures: Ezekiel 7:23
Make a chain: for the land is full of bloody crimes, and the city is full of violence.
Acts 25:16

To whom I answered, It is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die, before that he which is accused have the accusers face to face, and have licence to answer for himself concerning the crime laid against him.
For this is an heinous crime; yea, it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges.
Acts 25:27
For it seemeth to me unreasonable to send a prisoner, and not withal to signify the crimes laid against him.
corruption_summary: Sin and crime are either collapsed into one another or divorced entirely, and Scripture keeps them distinct without separating them.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors face each other here. The first collapses crime into sin and demands that the civil magistrate punish everything God forbids, which no biblical polity attempted; covetousness is forbidden in the Decalogue and no human court can try it. The second divorces them entirely, treating law as a merely social convention with no moral content, so that a thing is wrong because it is illegal rather than illegal because it is wrong. Job 31:11 holds the biblical position: adultery is an iniquity and a matter for the judges. The magistrate bears the sword under God, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of them that do well, and his jurisdiction is real and limited.

Acts 25 deserves more attention than it gets from Christians discussing law and justice. The procedural protections Festus describes — the accused meets his accusers face to face, knows the charge, and has licence to answer — are stated by a pagan Roman official and recorded approvingly. They are also, in substance, the requirements of the law of Moses, which demanded two or three witnesses and provided for the false accuser to bear the penalty he sought. Where those protections erode — where accusation functions as conviction, and a man learns the charge only from the crowd — something Scripture treats as basic justice has been lost, and Christians of all people should notice.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishpat damim, bloody judgments or crimes — Ezekiel 7:23; avon pelilim, an iniquity for the judges — Job 31:11; Greek aitia (G156) and egklema (G1462), a charge — Acts 25:16, 25:27.
roots_lines: Hebrew damim — bloods, bloodguilt; Ezekiel 7:23, of a land full of bloody crimes.
Hebrew pelilim — judges; Job 31:11, an iniquity to be punished by the judges.
Greek egklema (G1462) — an accusation, a charge laid; Acts 25:16 and Acts 23:29.
Greek aitia (G156) — a cause, an accusation; Acts 25:27, of the crimes to be signified.
Deuteronomy 19:15 gives the law's own procedural rule: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.
usage: “The land is full of bloody crimes, and the city is full of violence”.
“Have the accusers face to face, and have licence to answer for himself” — stated by a pagan governor.
“An heinous crime… an iniquity to be punished by the judges” — both at once.

pos: v. and n. (to remove a cause to a higher court; Paul's use of Roman citizenship to reach Caesar's judgment seat)
etymology: Latin appellare, to call upon or address. In Roman law the provocatio ad Caesarem was the citizen's right to have his case transferred out of a provincial court to the emperor — a right Paul possessed by birth and used deliberately.
biblical_def: Standing before Festus, with a proposal on the table to move his trial to Jerusalem where an ambush was waiting, Paul said: “I stand at Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged: to the Jews have I done no wrong, as thou very well knowest” (Acts 25:10), and then: “if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar” (Acts 25:11). Festus consulted his council and answered, “Hast thou appealed unto Caesar? unto Caesar shalt thou go” (Acts 25:12). The appeal was irreversible, and Agrippa afterwards observed as much: “This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar” (Acts 26:32). Paul explained his reasoning later in Rome without bitterness: “when the Jews spake against it, I was constrained to appeal unto Caesar; not that I had ought to accuse my nation of” (Acts 28:19). It was the appeal that carried the gospel to Rome at imperial expense, and Paul had long said he must see Rome. He used a legal right, and God used it to fulfil a purpose stated chapters earlier.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines appeal as to remove a cause from an inferior to a superior judge or court, and notes the practice among the Romans of appealing to the emperor.
webster_full: APPEAL, v.i. To refer to a superior judge or court, for the decision of a cause depending.
2. To refer to another for the decision of a question controverted.
APPEAL, n. The removal of a cause or suit from an inferior to a superior tribunal.
2. In the ancient Roman government, an appeal to the emperor, as the last resort.
TRIBUNAL, n. The seat of a judge; the bench on which a judge and his associates sit for administering justice.
scriptures: Acts 25:11

For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar.
Acts 25:12
Then Festus, when he had conferred with the council, answered, Hast thou appealed unto Caesar? unto Caesar shalt thou go.
Acts 26:32
Then said Agrippa unto Festus, This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar.
Acts 28:19
But when the Jews spake against it, I was constrained to appeal unto Caesar; not that I had ought to accuse my nation of.
corruption_summary: Using lawful protections is treated as a failure of faith, and Paul used every one available to him without apology.
corruption_paragraphs: A certain piety holds that a Christian under unjust treatment should simply submit and say nothing — that invoking a legal right shows a want of trust. Paul's conduct refutes it repeatedly. He appealed to Caesar; he told the magistrates at Philippi to come and fetch him out themselves; he informed the centurion at Jerusalem that he was a Roman before the scourging began. He also submitted to imprisonment, beating and death when the protections ran out. The two are not in tension: providence works through means, and a citizen's legal standing is one of the means God has provided. Paul used them, and when they failed he suffered without complaint.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty visible in the outcome. Agrippa's remark that Paul could have been freed if he had not appealed reads like a lament over a tactical blunder, and Luke records it deadpan at the end of the chapter. But the Lord had stood by Paul in Jerusalem and told him he must bear witness at Rome, and the appeal is what carried him there — escorted, fed and guarded at the empire's expense, to preach in his own hired house with no man forbidding him. What looked like a lost acquittal was the road to the commission. Providence commonly works this way, and it is usually only visible afterwards.
roots_summary: Greek epikaleomai (G1941), to call upon, to appeal — Acts 25:11, 25:12, 25:21, 25:25, 26:32, 28:19; bema (G968), a judgment seat — Acts 25:10.
roots_lines: Greek epikaleomai (G1941) — to call upon; in the middle voice, to appeal to a higher court; six times in Acts 25-28.
Greek bema (G968) — a raised place, a judgment seat; Acts 25:10, and 2 Corinthians 5:10 of the judgment seat of Christ.
Greek Sebastos (G4575) — Augustus, the imperial title; Acts 25:21, 25:25.
Latin provocatio — the Roman citizen's right of appeal to the emperor, which Paul held from birth.
Acts 23:11 gives the promise the appeal served: as thou hast testified of me in Jerusalem, so must thou bear witness also at Rome.
usage: “I appeal unto Caesar” — a legal right, used deliberately.
“Hast thou appealed unto Caesar? unto Caesar shalt thou go” — and it could not be undone.
“This man might have been set at liberty” — and would not have reached Rome.

pos: adj. (not tried or sentenced; the ground of Paul's two protests against being beaten without trial)
etymology: From un- and condemned, Latin condemnare, to sentence. The Greek akatakritos is a legal term: not having been judged, and therefore not liable to punishment.
biblical_def: Twice Paul raises the same objection, and both times it stops proceedings. At Philippi, after a night in the stocks, the magistrates sent word to release them quietly: “But Paul said unto them, They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans, and have cast us into prison; and now do they thrust us out privily? nay verily; but let them come themselves and fetch us out” (Acts 16:37). The effect was immediate: “the serjeants told these words unto the magistrates: and they feared, when they heard that they were Romans” (Acts 16:38). At Jerusalem, bound and about to be examined by scourging, he put it as a question: “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?” (Acts 22:25), and the centurion went straight to the chief captain (Acts 22:26). Two things are worth noting. Paul raised the objection after the beating at Philippi, not before, and his concern was public vindication for the infant church he was leaving behind, not his own comfort. At Jerusalem he raised it before, and it spared him. He knew the law and used it precisely.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines uncondemned as not condemned, not judged guilty, and condemn as to pronounce to be utterly wrong or to sentence to punishment.
webster_full: UNCONDEMNED, a. Not condemned; not judged guilty.
CONDEMN, v.t. To pronounce to be utterly wrong; to utter a sentence of disapprobation against.
2. To determine or judge to be wrong, or guilty; to disallow.
3. To sentence to punishment; to utter sentence against judicially.
SCOURGE, v.t. To whip severely; to lash; to punish with severity.
scriptures: Acts 16:37

But Paul said unto them, They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans, and have cast us into prison; and now do they thrust us out privily? nay verily; but let them come themselves and fetch us out.
Acts 22:25
And as they bound him with thongs, Paul said unto the centurion that stood by, Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?
Acts 16:38
And the serjeants told these words unto the magistrates: and they feared, when they heard that they were Romans.
Acts 22:26
When the centurion heard that, he went and told the chief captain, saying, Take heed what thou doest: for this man is a Roman.
corruption_summary: Punishment before trial is a recurring temptation of every age, and Paul's objection names it in a single word.
corruption_paragraphs: Beaten openly uncondemned is a precise charge: the sequence was reversed. Punishment came first and judgment never came at all. Roman law forbade it in the case of a citizen, and the law of Moses forbade it generally — the accused meets his accusers, witnesses are examined, and only then is sentence pronounced. Every era finds reasons to reverse the order when the accusation is grave enough or the accused unpopular enough, and the reversal is always defended as urgency. Scripture's consistent position is that the order is the protection, and that a society which punishes before it judges has abandoned justice regardless of how guilty the accused turns out to be.

Paul's two uses of the objection show a wisdom worth imitating. At Jerusalem he spoke before the scourging and was spared; at Philippi he said nothing until afterwards, and then refused a quiet release, demanding that the magistrates come publicly. The reason was not wounded pride. He was leaving behind a new congregation in a Roman colony, including a jailer and his household baptised that night, and a public acknowledgment that the preachers had been wrongly beaten protected those believers after he left. He absorbed the injury and then used the law for the sake of the church, which is a different thing from using it for himself.
roots_summary: Greek akatakritos (G178), uncondemned, without trial — Acts 16:37, 22:25, its only occurrences; mastizo (G3147), to scourge — Acts 22:25.
roots_lines: Greek akatakritos (G178) — not judged, uncondemned; Acts 16:37 and 22:25 only.
Greek demosia (G1219) — publicly, openly; Acts 16:37, of the manner of the beating.
Greek lathra (G2977) — privily, secretly; Acts 16:37, of the release Paul refused.
Greek mastizo (G3147) — to scourge with the whip; Acts 22:25, the examination Paul stopped.
Deuteronomy 19:18-19 supplies the law's protection: the judges shall make diligent inquisition, and a false witness bears the penalty he intended.
usage: “They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans” — the sequence was reversed.
“Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?”
He absorbed the injury, then used the law for the church he was leaving.

pos: adj. (contrary to reason, or without reason; used by Festus of a procedural absurdity and by Paul of men from whom he asks to be delivered)
etymology: From un- and reasonable, Latin ratio. In Acts 25:27 the Greek is alogos, without reason, illogical; in 2 Thessalonians 3:2 the word is atopos, literally out of place, hence improper or absurd.
biblical_def: Festus, having to send Paul to Rome and unable to formulate a charge, says: “For it seemeth to me unreasonable to send a prisoner, and not withal to signify the crimes laid against him” (Acts 25:27). It is an admission of the whole case's emptiness — the governor cannot state what the man is accused of, and knows how that will look at the imperial court. Paul uses a different word for a different thing when he asks the Thessalonians to pray “that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith” (2 Thessalonians 3:2). The Greek there means out of place, absurd, perverse — men with whom argument does not work, because the obstacle is not intellectual. The clause that follows explains it: for all men have not faith. Opposition to the gospel is not finally a failure of information. And Paul does not end on the danger: “But the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep you from evil” (2 Thessalonians 3:3). Men are unreasonable; the Lord is faithful; the sentence turns on that contrast.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unreasonable as not agreeable to reason, exceeding the bounds of reason, immoderate, and also not conformable to reason in conduct.
webster_full: UNREASONABLE, a. Not agreeable to reason.
2. Exceeding the bounds of reason; claiming or insisting on more than is fit; as an unreasonable demand.
3. Immoderate; as unreasonable bulk.
4. Irrational; as unreasonable creatures.
ABSURD, a. Opposed to manifest truth; inconsistent with reason or the plain dictates of common sense.
scriptures: Acts 25:27
For it seemeth to me unreasonable to send a prisoner, and not withal to signify the crimes laid against him.
2 Thessalonians 3:2
And that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith.
2 Thessalonians 3:3
But the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep you from evil.
Acts 25:16

To whom I answered, It is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die, before that he which is accused have the accusers face to face, and have licence to answer for himself concerning the crime laid against him.
corruption_summary: Unbelief is treated as an argument to be won, and Paul locates the obstacle where Scripture always locates it — in the will, not the intellect.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Thessalonians 3:2 is a short course in apologetics. Paul asks for deliverance from unreasonable and wicked men and then gives the diagnosis in five words: for all men have not faith. The men are not merely mistaken; they are without faith, and no quantity of argument supplies what only God gives. This does not make reasoning useless — Paul reasoned in the synagogues every sabbath, and Peter commands a reason for the hope that is in us. It means that argument is a means and not the cause, and that a Christian who has answered every objection and met a hardened response has encountered exactly what the apostle describes rather than a failure of technique.

Acts 25:27 shows the other side, where the unreasonableness is procedural and a pagan official is the one who notices it. Festus cannot name the crime and finds it absurd to forward a prisoner without one. Persecution frequently has this quality: enormous energy directed at a man whose offence, when someone finally tries to write it down, evaporates. Luke lets the point make itself — three separate officials in these chapters say Paul has done nothing worthy of death or bonds, and he is sent to Rome anyway. The record is not merely biographical; it is the earliest legal defence of Christianity, written down by a careful historian.
roots_summary: Greek alogos (G249), without reason, absurd — Acts 25:27, 2 Peter 2:12, Jude 10; atopos (G824), out of place, perverse — 2 Thessalonians 3:2, Luke 23:41, Acts 28:6.
roots_lines: Greek alogos (G249) — without reason, irrational; Acts 25:27, and 2 Peter 2:12 of natural brute beasts.
Greek atopos (G824) — out of place, improper, absurd; 2 Thessalonians 3:2, and Luke 23:41 where the thief says Christ hath done nothing amiss.
Greek pistis (G4102) — faith; 2 Thessalonians 3:2, all men have not faith.
Greek pistos (G4103) — faithful; 2 Thessalonians 3:3, the deliberate answering word in the next verse.
1 Corinthians 2:14 supplies the doctrine: the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God, neither can he know them.
usage: “Unreasonable to send a prisoner, and not withal to signify the crimes” — a governor with no charge.
“Delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith”.
“But the Lord is faithful” — the contrast the sentence turns on.

pos: v. (told beforehand; of the Lord's warning to His disciples and of the prophets' united testimony to the days of Christ)
etymology: From fore- (before) and told. It renders Greek proereo in Mark 13:23, to say beforehand, and prokataggello in Acts 3:24, to announce in advance.
biblical_def: At the end of His warning about false christs and false prophets who would shew signs and wonders to seduce, the Lord says: “But take ye heed: behold, I have foretold you all things” (Mark 13:23). The forewarning is itself the protection — a disciple who has been told in advance is not to be surprised or swept away, and the command attached is take ye heed. Peter uses the word for the whole prophetic witness: “Yea, and all the prophets from Samuel and those that follow after, as many as have spoken, have likewise foretold of these days” (Acts 3:24). The claim is comprehensive — not that a few texts happen to fit, but that the entire line of prophets spoke of the days that had now arrived. He had said the same of the sufferings a few verses earlier: “those things, which God before had shewed by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he hath so fulfilled” (Acts 3:18). Prophecy in the apostolic use is not primarily a puzzle to be decoded but a testimony already given, whose fulfilment vindicates both the Speaker and the Scriptures He spoke through.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines foretell as to predict, to tell before an event happens, and to foretoken or previously declare.
webster_full: FORETELL, v.t. To predict; to tell before an event happens; to prophesy.
2. To foretoken; to foreshow.
FORETOLD, pp. Predicted; foreshown.
PROPHECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come.
FULFIL, v.t. To accomplish; to perform; to complete; to answer in event or by an event.
scriptures: Mark 13:23
But take ye heed: behold, I have foretold you all things.
Acts 3:24
Yea, and all the prophets from Samuel and those that follow after, as many as have spoken, have likewise foretold of these days.
Acts 3:18
But those things, which God before had shewed by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he hath so fulfilled.
Deuteronomy 18:22

When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him.
corruption_summary: Prophecy is treated as a code for charting future events, and the New Testament treats it as testimony already given about Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter says that all the prophets from Samuel onward foretold these days — the days of the crucified and risen Christ and the gospel going out from Jerusalem. That is how the apostles read the Old Testament, and it is a very different practice from the modern habit of mining the prophets for a timetable of events still future. Dispensational systems, unknown before the nineteenth century, have made prophecy chiefly a matter of charts and dates, and in doing so have quietly displaced its own stated subject. Whatever a reader concludes about the millennium — and Reformed orthodoxy has held more than one view — the prophets' announced theme, on apostolic authority, is Christ and His sufferings and the glory that should follow.

Mark 13:23 supplies the pastoral purpose of prediction, which is almost the opposite of curiosity. The Lord foretells deception, persecution and upheaval, and the application He draws is take ye heed. Foreknowledge of trouble is given so that believers will not be shaken by it when it comes, and specifically so that signs and wonders performed by false christs will not carry them away. A church absorbed in decoding current events has usually stopped doing the thing the passage actually commands, which is to watch, to hold fast, and to be unsurprised.
roots_summary: Greek proereo (G4280), to say beforehand — Mark 13:23, 2 Corinthians 13:2; prokataggello (G4293), to announce beforehand — Acts 3:24, 7:52; prophemi, the root of prophecy.
roots_lines: Greek proereo (G4280) — to speak before; Mark 13:23, and Galatians 1:9 of what Paul had said already.
Greek prokataggello (G4293) — to announce beforehand; Acts 3:24, and Acts 7:52 of the prophets who shewed before of the coming of the Just One.
Greek propascho and pathema — the sufferings foretold; Acts 3:18, that Christ should suffer.
Greek blepo (G991) — to look, take heed; Mark 13:23, the command attached to the foretelling.
1 Peter 1:11 states the prophets' own subject: the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.
usage: “Behold, I have foretold you all things” — and the command is take ye heed.
“All the prophets from Samuel… have likewise foretold of these days”.
Prophecy's announced subject is Christ, on apostolic authority.

pos: n. and v. (a violent attack; the attempt on Paul and Barnabas at Iconium, and the attack the Jews were licensed to resist under Ahasuerus)
etymology: Old French asaut, from Latin assultus, a leaping upon. An assault is a rush — sudden, physical, and short of a siege.
biblical_def: At Iconium the opposition moved from argument to violence: “And when there was an assault made both of the Gentiles, and also of the Jews with their rulers, to use them despitefully, and to stone them” (Acts 14:5). The apostles' response is recorded without embarrassment: “They were ware of it, and fled unto Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and unto the region that lieth round about” (Acts 14:6) — and preached the gospel there. Flight from an assault is not treated as cowardice; the Lord had told them, when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another. The other use is the decree of Ahasuerus after Haman's fall, granting the Jews the right of self-defence: the king granted them “to gather themselves together, and to stand for their life, to destroy, to slay, and to cause to perish, all the power of the people and province that would assault them, both little ones and women” (Esther 8:11). The earlier decree could not be revoked under Persian law, so a second decree was issued permitting resistance. Deliverance in Esther comes without a single miracle and without the name of God appearing in the book — which is the point of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines assault as an attack or violent onset, and in law an unlawful setting upon one's person.
webster_full: ASSAULT, n. An attack or violent onset, whether by an individual, a company, or an army.
2. An attack by hostile words or measures.
3. In law, an unlawful setting upon one's person; an attempt or offer to beat another.
ASSAULT, v.t. To attack or fall upon by violence, or with a hostile intention.
DESPITEFULLY, adv. With despite; maliciously; contemptuously.
scriptures: Acts 14:5
And when there was an assault made both of the Gentiles, and also of the Jews with their rulers, to use them despitefully, and to stone them,
Acts 14:6
They were ware of it, and fled unto Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and unto the region that lieth round about:
Esther 8:11

Wherein the king granted the Jews which were in every city to gather themselves together, and to stand for their life, to destroy, to slay, and to cause to perish, all the power of the people and province that would assault them, both little ones and women, and to take the spoil of them for a prey,
2 Thessalonians 3:3
But the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep you from evil.
corruption_summary: Courage is defined as never withdrawing, and the apostles withdrew as a matter of course and kept preaching somewhere else.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 14:6 records the apostles fleeing an assault, and Luke reports it as ordinary prudence in obedience to the Lord's own instruction. A piety that treats every withdrawal as compromise has not read the narrative: Paul left Damascus in a basket, left Iconium for Lystra, was sent away from Berea by the brethren, and was later urged by friends not to enter the theatre at Ephesus. He also stayed and was stoned at Lystra, and went back into the city the next day. There is no rule that resolves this into a formula. There is a Lord who is served both by staying and by leaving, and the mark of the difference is the work, not the reputation of the man doing it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Esther's doctrine of providence. The book contains no miracle, no prophet, no mention of the name of God, and no explicit prayer — and it is the clearest account in Scripture of how deliverance ordinarily comes: a sleepless night, a court record read aloud, a decree permitting a people to stand for their life. Christians who look for God's hand only in the extraordinary will miss most of what He does. The right of a people to defend their own little ones and women against assault is granted here by a pagan king, and the Bible records the deliverance as God's work without ever saying so.
roots_summary: Greek horme (G3730), an impulse or assault — Acts 14:5, James 3:4; Hebrew tsur and related terms for besieging or attacking — Esther 8:11.
roots_lines: Greek horme (G3730) — a rush, impulse, violent assault; Acts 14:5, and James 3:4 of the helm turning a ship.
Greek hubrizo (G5195) — to treat despitefully, insult; Acts 14:5, of what the crowd intended.
Hebrew amad al nephesh — to stand for the life; Esther 8:11, the right granted to the Jews.
Hebrew Purim — the feast established to commemorate the deliverance; Esther 9:26.
Matthew 10:23 gives the Lord's own instruction: when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another.
usage: “An assault made… to use them despitefully, and to stone them” — and they fled and preached elsewhere.
“To gather themselves together, and to stand for their life”.
Esther records a deliverance without a miracle and without naming God.

pos: adj. (extended, reached out; of the arm by which God brought Israel from Egypt — and, in Jeremiah, by which He fought against them)
etymology: From out and stretched, rendering Hebrew netuyah, the passive participle of natah, to stretch out. It is joined almost always to zeroa, an arm, or yad, a hand.
biblical_def: The phrase is the standing formula for the Exodus. In the confession made at the offering of firstfruits: “And the LORD brought us forth out of Egypt with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with great terribleness, and with signs, and with wonders” (Deuteronomy 26:8). Moses uses it in the great rhetorical question about whether any god ever took a nation from the midst of another nation “by a mighty hand, and by a stretched out arm” (Deuteronomy 4:34), and it grounds the fourth commandment in Deuteronomy's version: “remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD thy God brought thee out thence through a mighty hand and by a stretched out arm: therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee to keep the sabbath day” (Deuteronomy 5:15). Then Jeremiah turns the formula against the nation, and the reversal is deliberate and terrible: “And I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm, even in anger, and in fury, and in great wrath” (Jeremiah 21:5). The same arm, the same vocabulary, aimed the other way. Jeremiah also uses it of creation and of God's right to dispose of the nations (Jeremiah 27:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines outstretched as extended, spread out, and stretch as to extend, to reach forth, to exert to the utmost.
webster_full: OUTSTRETCHED, pp. Extended; stretched out; expanded.
STRETCH, v.t. To draw out to greater length; to extend in a line.
2. To extend in breadth; to spread.
3. To reach out; to extend; as, to stretch out the arm.
ARM, n. Figuratively, power, might; as the secular arm; the arm of the LORD.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 26:8
And the LORD brought us forth out of Egypt with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with great terribleness, and with signs, and with wonders:
Deuteronomy 5:15

And remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD thy God brought thee out thence through a mighty hand and by a stretched out arm: therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee to keep the sabbath day.
Jeremiah 21:5
And I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm, even in anger, and in fury, and in great wrath.
Jeremiah 27:5
I have made the earth, the man and the beast that are upon the ground, by my great power and by my outstretched arm, and have given it unto whom it seemed meet unto me.
corruption_summary: God's power is assumed to be permanently on one side, and Jeremiah records the formula of deliverance turned against the delivered.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 21:5 is one of the most alarming verses in the prophets precisely because of its vocabulary. Every Israelite knew an outstretched hand and a strong arm; it was the language of the Exodus, recited at the firstfruits and attached to the sabbath commandment. Jeremiah takes the formula and puts it in God's mouth as a declaration of war against Jerusalem. A people may possess a true history of divine deliverance and find the same power arrayed against them, and no covenant privilege prevents it. Every nation and church that assumes God's arm is permanently committed to its side because of what He did in an earlier generation should read this verse slowly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the way Deuteronomy grounds obedience. The sabbath command in Deuteronomy 5 is not argued from utility or from need for rest; it is argued from redemption — remember that thou wast a servant… therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee. That is the structure of biblical ethics throughout: the indicative of what God has done, then the imperative of what His people are to do. Preaching that issues commands without rehearsing the deliverance produces moralism, and preaching that rehearses the deliverance and never issues commands produces sentiment. Deuteronomy 5:15 does both in one sentence.
roots_summary: Hebrew natah, to stretch out — the participle netuyah in Deuteronomy 4:34, 5:15, 26:8, Jeremiah 21:5, 27:5; joined to zeroa, an arm, and yad chazaqah, a mighty hand.
roots_lines: Hebrew natah — to stretch out, extend; its participle gives the standing formula of the Exodus.
Hebrew zeroa — an arm, and figuratively strength; Deuteronomy 26:8, Isaiah 53:1 of the arm of the LORD revealed.
Hebrew yad chazaqah — a mighty hand; the constant companion of the outstretched arm.
Hebrew mora gadol — great terribleness; Deuteronomy 26:8, one of the five terms in the confession.
Isaiah 53:1 asks the question the formula finally answers: to whom is the arm of the LORD revealed?
usage: “With a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm” — the standing formula of the Exodus.
“Remember that thou wast a servant… therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee”.
“I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand” — the same arm, reversed.
